CPSR: Options on the S&P 500 structured to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each March, with gains capped as the cost of protection. It suits holders who stay the full period, since the protection is designed around that fixed window.
BREM: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies, mostly borrowed in hard currencies like dollars and euros, picked actively by BlackRock. Active management tries to dodge the weakest countries, a real risk in emerging market debt, while collecting its higher income.
GEMD: Bonds from emerging market governments and state-linked issuers, all in US dollars, screened for good governance and solid fundamentals. The screens aim to keep the higher income of emerging market debt while avoiding its most troubled borrowers.
JULM: Options on the S&P 500 seeking the deepest loss protection available over a year starting in July, as its Max Buffer name promises. Maximum protection means minimal participation in rallies, so this is capital preservation first and growth a distant second.
BIGY: Fifty of America's biggest companies, technology giants at the front, with covered call options sold against them to generate income. The Target 12 name points to the high payout it aims for, reached by giving up part of the stocks' gains.
SNAV: A tactical fund that navigates among the sectors of the S&P 500, shifting money toward whichever industries look strongest, through sector and index funds. It accepts full stock market risk, so the navigation is about which sectors to ride, not whether to be in stocks.
CPSN: Options on the S&P 500 built to protect against losses over an outcome period resetting each November, trading away part of any gain for the shield. Bought at the wrong moment the protection can differ, so it is designed for buy-and-hold use.
YSPC: An income fund built on indirect exposure to SpaceX, the private rocket company, using a synthetic covered call strategy on instruments tied to its value. Because SpaceX does not trade publicly, the exposure is indirect and hard to value, making this a speculative oddity.
PQJA: Options on the Nasdaq-100 built to absorb about the first eighth of a loss over a one-year period starting in January, matching its Buffer 12 name. Buffering tech-heavy growth stocks tames their famous swings, with capped gains as the cost.
OEFA: Dividend-paying companies across Europe that pass quality, steadiness and yield tests, spanning drug makers, industrial giants and banks. It favors reliable payers over the highest yields, aiming for international income with fewer nasty surprises.
DRES: US companies set to gain as supply chains come home: railroads, building material makers, industrial and energy firms that rebuild domestic capacity. It is GMO's bet on deglobalization and onshoring, a theme fund tied to trade and industrial policy.
YOLO: Companies that make most of their money from marijuana and hemp: cannabis growers, dispensary chains and related suppliers, picked actively. It is a pure bet on legal cannabis spreading, and the industry's legal and banking troubles make it one of the wildest stock funds around.
ASMF: A managed futures program trading trends across stock, bond, currency and commodity markets worldwide, using futures and forwards. AlphaSimplex's models ride sustained moves in either direction, aiming to profit in crises when ordinary portfolios usually suffer together.
DWMF: Companies from developed markets outside the US and Canada, selected by a model weighing several return factors like value, quality and momentum. Banks are the biggest group, and the multifactor tilt aims to beat a plain international index over time.
YGLD: Leveraged exposure to gold through futures, targeting up to about one and a half times the gold price move, with option selling on other markets to add income. The leverage magnifies gold's swings, so it is a punchier, more complex way to hold the metal.
SPIT: Companies in special situations, events like spinoffs, restructurings or turnarounds that can unlock hidden value, mostly mid-sized and smaller firms. Event-driven picking like this depends on the managers reading corporate dramas well, and situations can take years to play out.
MARZ: Options on the S&P 500 that cushion part of a market fall over an outcome period restarting each March, in exchange for some upside. It is part of a monthly series of structured outcome funds, each with its own starting point and protection level.
GOLS: Owners of sports teams, leagues and live entertainment: the companies behind the games, races and shows people pay to watch. It is a playful but real bet on live events and media rights, an asset class usually reserved for billionaires.
LITP: Lithium miners and explorers from around the world, the companies digging out the key ingredient of rechargeable batteries. It is a leveraged play on electric vehicle demand in effect, since lithium prices, and these small miners, swing violently with the battery cycle.
DFTT: Thirty of America's hundred largest stocks, chosen by price momentum under a formula that also manages risk, currently led by chip and drug companies. Momentum means it buys what has been winning, which works until trends reverse suddenly.
HELX: Companies advancing genomics: DNA testing firms, gene therapy developers and the labs and toolmakers behind them. It is a bet that reading and editing genes transforms medicine, concentrated in smaller biotech names whose fortunes turn on research results.
SEPM: Options on the S&P 500 that aim for the maximum buffer against losses over a year starting in September, per the Max Buffer label. The trade is stark: near-total shelter from falls, with only a small slice of any rally kept.
QBIG: The very largest companies in the Nasdaq-100, the mega-sized top of the growth index, gathered into one concentrated fund. It doubles down on the giants that already dominate the Nasdaq, so it is technology-heavy and rises or falls with a handful of names.
LDEM: Emerging market companies that score well on environmental, social and governance measures, led by Asian chip makers, internet firms and banks. The ESG screen trims the usual emerging market lineup, though it still swings like one, with extra movement from currencies.
APRZ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to absorb part of a decline over an outcome period that restarts each April, while surrendering a slice of gains. The actively managed structure tries to keep that protection intact as markets move during the period.
BALQ: Nasdaq-listed companies, dominated by big technology names, with an options program designed to turn their price moves into premium income. It aims to keep much of the growth of the Nasdaq while paying income along the way, accepting less upside in the strongest rallies.
BUIL: Companies rebuilding America's infrastructure: the builders, equipment makers, solar and materials firms behind new roads, grids and factories. It is a theme bet on the domestic building boom, led by industrial and technology suppliers rather than the utilities most infrastructure funds favor.
TMED: Health care companies of every kind: drug makers, insurers, device firms, lab tool suppliers and distributors, picked actively by researchers who specialize in the field. A single-industry fund like this can outrun the market when medicine advances, and stumble when politics turns on drug prices.
PSCC: Small companies in consumer staples: food makers, grocery distributors and household goods firms serving everyday needs. Staples are usually the calmest corner of the market, but small size adds wiggle, so this is defensive with a small-company twist.
NITE: A concentrated handful of about twenty US growth stocks, led by big technology, consumer and financial names, picked with conviction. With so few holdings, each one matters a lot, so it will look and behave very differently from a broad index fund.
AMZW: Built around one stock, Amazon, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move while paying income weekly. It is a trading tool on a single giant company, with leverage resetting every week and swings to match.
SNTQ: Nasdaq-100 exposure built synthetically from options, with US Treasuries making up most of the fund as backing. This engineered approach aims to reshape the ups and downs of big tech stocks, though the outcome depends on the option positions in place at any time.
TOPC: The S&P 500 with every company capped at 3 percent of the fund, so the mega-sized tech giants count for far less than usual. The cap spreads influence across all 500 names, making it a more even-handed version of the classic big-company index.
ISTM: A basket of futures on metals used heavily in rebuilding industry: power grids, AI data centers, factories, energy systems and defense. It holds futures rather than mining shares, so it follows metal prices directly, with the sharp moves commodities are known for.
MNZL: Large US companies that pass Shariah compliance screening, which rules out conventional banks, alcohol and other non-permissible businesses, leaving technology dominant. It gives Muslim investors a broad market fund aligned with Islamic principles, with the side effect of no bank exposure.
LOGO: Leading consumer brands from around the world, the companies behind what people buy, eat, watch and wear, picked actively. Brand strength is the thesis: famous names can charge more and keep customers, making this a quality-tilted bet on global spending.
DECP: Options on the S&P 500 meant to absorb about the first eighth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in December, as the Buffer 12 name says. A moderate cushion for cautious investors, leaving more upside than the deepest buffer funds.
GFGF: High quality companies favored by about twenty famous long-term investors whose portfolios the managers follow, bought at what they judge reasonable prices. It outsources stock picking to proven gurus, leaning toward big technology and financial names those investors love.
HXE: A mix of US stock funds, from quality and large company funds to small caps, wrapped in an adaptive hedging program. The hedge can pull a large share into cash when risk looks high, so its stock exposure changes a lot over time.
MAYZ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to soften part of any market drop over an outcome period that restarts each May, at the cost of capped participation. Investors who buy mid-period get different protection than those who start at the reset date.
NRSH: Companies positioned for nearshoring, the shift of supply chains toward North America: industrial landlords, logistics and transport firms across the US, Mexico and Canada. It bets factories moving closer to home lift these businesses, a theme tied to trade policy.
XISE: Options on the S&P 500 that combine a loss buffer with premium income, paying out option premiums as regular income over a year to September. It trades stock market thrills for a paycheck style return, with gains limited by design.
ASHS: Five hundred smaller companies listed on mainland China's own exchanges, spread across technology, industry and materials. These A-shares are the domestic Chinese market foreigners rarely reach directly, with all the volatility and government influence that comes with it.
FDNI: Internet companies from outside the US: online marketplaces, streaming, social platforms and digital services across emerging and developed markets. It skips American tech entirely, which is the point, offering the rest of the world's internet in one fund.
NURE: Property trusts whose leases are short: apartment buildings, hotels and rental home companies that can raise rents quickly. Short leases let landlords reprice with inflation, which is the appeal, though occupancy swings hit hotels and apartments fast in downturns.
RSSE: Options on an equal-weight version of the S&P 500, where every company counts the same, with a buffer against part of any loss over a year to September. Equal weighting softens the mega-cap dominance of the usual index, and gains are capped in exchange for the cushion.
EMPB: An algorithm-driven long-short fund holding sector funds it expects to beat the market, plus bets against things like long-term bonds. Going both long and short makes it a hedge-fund-style product whose results hinge on the algorithm's calls.
PVI: Municipal bonds whose interest rates reset daily, weekly or monthly, issued by states, cities and public agencies across the US. Floating rates keep the price nearly still when market rates move, and the income is tax-exempt, making it a calm, cash-like corner of the muni market.
FEBZ: Options on the S&P 500 that take part of a market loss for you over an outcome period restarting each February, paid for by giving up some gains. One of twelve monthly starting points in its series, letting investors choose when their year begins.
OARK: A synthetic covered call fund built on an innovation fund of disruptive growth companies, using options to harvest their price swings as income. The payouts can be large because the underlying stocks are volatile, and the strategy caps gains while keeping most losses.
